title: The Accumulation of Score Estimation Error in Diffusion Models
claim: Local error contributions concentrate sharply near the data end of the diffusion process and vary systematically with the noise schedule.
layout: single panel, log-scale line plot, shaded bands, legend top-right
description: A single line plot titled 'step error density'. The x-axis is OU time τ from 0 to about 5. The y-axis is step error per OU time on a log scale, from 10^-2 to 10^3. Four colored curves with dot markers and translucent confidence bands show four noise schedules: Linear (blue), Quadratic (orange), Cosine (green) and Uniform-logSNR (red). All curves spike steeply at τ near 0, reaching about 10^2 to 10^3, with green highest. They then drop to roughly 0.2 to 0.5 and decline slowly toward about 0.05 to 0.2 at τ=5. Cosine stays above the others through the middle range. Dashed gridlines, a top-right legend, and spines only on the left and bottom. The eye goes first to the tall spike at the left edge.
caption: Step-wise error density induced by learned scoreestimation errors. For each schedule, the empirical scoreestimation errors are evaluated through our error-propagation formula to illustrate their local contributions to the final W2 bound.
abstract: Diffusion models are widely used for high-quality generation, but their performance is sensitive to the accuracy of the estimated score. We first derive a stepwise Wasserstein error bound in a Gaussian-mixture setting, where the score admits a closed-form structure, and the score Hessian can be controlled explicitly, leading to sharp Wasserstein estimates. We then extend the analysis to general data distributions, which yields a more general but typically looser upper bound. This general bound can be sharpened under mild regularity: when the initial distribution has a globally Lipschitz score, the curvature contribution at small times is uniformly bounded, avoiding the worst-case blow-up. The results hold for both variance-preserving (VP) and variance-exploding (VE) diffusions, and apply to both the reverse-time SDE and the associated probability-flow ODE.
